analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the federal estate tax never advanced past its referral to the Ways and Means Committee and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the federal estate tax (often called the "death tax"), along with the gift tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, retroactive to the start of 1999. The estate tax only applies to very large estates, so repealing it would chiefly benefit the heirs of the wealthiest families while reducing federal revenue that other taxpayers would have to make up. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of the wealthiest families would gain the most, since the estate tax only applies to large estates — in practice, a small share of multi-million-dollar estates. Very wealthy families could transfer fortunes across generations without the transfer taxes that currently apply. Estate planning professionals would also retain a client base, though the tax-driven part of their work would shrink.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for everyone.
It applies the repeal to all deaths and gifts after December 31, 1998, so even estates settled shortly after introduction would escape the tax.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue from estate and gift taxes — tens of billions of dollars a year in the late 1990s — would disappear, meaning either larger deficits or higher taxes on everyone else. Ordinary taxpayers would ultimately bear that cost through debt or other taxes, with no offsetting benefit.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes with no replacement revenue, adding to deficits or forcing cuts or higher taxes elsewhere.
The repeal applies retroactively to transfers after December 31, 1998, maximizing the immediate windfall to large estates rather than phasing in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a clean full repeal with no replacement revenue, so its entire cost — hundreds of billions over a decade in general-knowledge terms — would have fallen on general taxpayers or the deficit while the benefit went to the heirs of the largest estates. Because it died, no benefit was delivered either; a defensible case for relieving family farms and small businesses could have been designed far more narrowly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 15, 1999 by Rep. Max Sandlin and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
It attracted only one cosponsor, a Republican, in the House.

No further action was taken: the bill sat in committee with no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate counterpart activity in the record, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal estate tax survived, so heirs of the largest estates continued paying it; no interest gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; the estate tax survived

for.name: Rep. Max Sandlin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 15, 1999 and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat with a single Republican cosponsor, so no clear party pattern can be read from this bill's short life.

industries.note: The estate tax applies only to large estates, so a full repeal is a direct windfall to families holding the greatest wealth and a way to pass fortunes across generations untaxed.

industries.industry: Estate planning lawyers and wealth advisors
industries.note: Although they earn fees helping families navigate the tax, its repeal would not harm the industry's client base; the bill removes the tax but not the demand for transferring large fortunes.
